name: Cable External Rotation (Elbow at Side)
rom_notes: Stand side-on to a low/mid cable, upper arm pinned to the ribs with the elbow bent 90 degrees and a rolled towel in the armpit to keep ~20 degrees abduction. Rotate the forearm outward away from the belly through a full arc, then control back across the body. Keep the wrist neutral so the cuff (not the forearm) does the work.
regional_bias: posterior rotator cuff (infraspinatus/teres minor) at the elbow-by-side angle; continuous cable tension loads the full arc better than a dumbbell
cues: Pin the elbow to your side (towel in the armpit), keep the forearm horizontal, and rotate only at the shoulder. Light load, no torso English; this is prehab/cuff-balance work, not a heavy pressing accessory.

name: Band External Rotation (Elbow at Side)
rom_notes: Anchor a band at elbow height, stand side-on with the upper arm against the ribs and elbow bent 90 degrees. Rotate the forearm outward against the ascending band tension, pause, and return under control. Towel in the armpit keeps the slight abduction that off-loads the joint.
regional_bias: posterior cuff (infraspinatus/teres minor); band tension is ascending (hardest at full external rotation) where the cuff is shortened
cues: Same elbow-pinned mechanics as the cable version but portable; choose a light band so the cuff, not momentum, completes the last few degrees. Ideal warm-up and travel option.

name: Cable External Rotation at 90-Degree Abduction
rom_notes: Set the cable at shoulder height, abduct the upper arm to 90 degrees with the elbow bent 90 degrees (the 'L' or 90/90 position). From a forearm-forward/down start, rotate the forearm up and back into full external rotation, then lower under control. Replicates the cocking phase of a throw and trains the cuff at the abducted angle where it is most vulnerable.
regional_bias: posterior cuff (infraspinatus/teres minor) in the abducted/overhead-relevant position; complements the elbow-at-side angle for fuller cuff coverage
cues: Keep the upper arm parallel to the floor the whole set; rotate at the shoulder, don't let the elbow drop. Light load and strict tempo — this abducted angle is where heavy/sloppy reps irritate the cuff.

name: Side-Lying Dumbbell External Rotation
rom_notes: Lie on your side, top arm's upper arm resting on the ribs, elbow bent 90 degrees, dumbbell held with the forearm across the belly. Rotate the forearm upward to point toward the ceiling, then lower under control. Gravity loads the mid-arc; a towel under the elbow keeps the slight abduction. Hardest at the top of the rotation.
regional_bias: posterior cuff (infraspinatus/teres minor); free-weight version peaks resistance near the top of external rotation and is light by necessity
cues: Keep the elbow glued to your side and lift only by rotating the shoulder; do not let the dumbbell swing or the torso roll back. Very light load (often 2-5 kg) — the cuff fatigues fast.

name: Full-Can Raise (Supraspinatus)
rom_notes: Raise the arms in the scapular plane (about 30 degrees forward of the frontal plane) with the thumbs pointing up ('full can', externally rotated) to roughly shoulder height. The thumbs-up/externally-rotated path biases the supraspinatus while sparing the subacromial space, unlike the thumbs-down 'empty can' which is more impinging. Stop near shoulder level; do not shrug or arch.
regional_bias: supraspinatus (initiates abduction in the scapular plane); the externally-rotated full-can path is the impingement-safer way to load it directly
cues: Thumbs up, raise in the scapular plane (45 degrees between front and side), stop at shoulder height. Light load; the goal is cuff initiation and stability, so keep the traps quiet and avoid swinging.

name: Cable Internal Rotation (Elbow at Side)
rom_notes: Stand side-on to the cable, upper arm pinned to the ribs and elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm starting out to the side (in external rotation). Rotate the forearm inward across the belly against the cable, then control back out to the stretched position. Towel in the armpit keeps the slight abduction. Continuous tension loads the full inward arc.
regional_bias: subscapularis (anterior cuff) at the elbow-by-side angle; internal rotators are strong, but this isolates the deep cuff component away from the lats/pecs
cues: Elbow glued to the side, rotate the forearm in toward the navel using the shoulder, not by leaning. Control the eccentric out to a stretch. Pair with external rotation for cuff balance.

name: Band Internal Rotation (Elbow at Side)
rom_notes: Anchor a band at elbow height, stand side-on with the upper arm against the ribs and elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm starting out to the side. Rotate the forearm inward across the belly against the ascending band tension, then return under control to the stretch. Towel in the armpit maintains the slight abduction.
regional_bias: subscapularis (anterior cuff); band tension peaks at full internal rotation where the subscapularis is shortened
cues: Portable cuff-balance work; keep the elbow pinned and rotate only at the shoulder. Light band, strict tempo, full controlled return to the lengthened position.

name: Lying Dumbbell Internal Rotation
rom_notes: Lie on the same side as the working arm with that upper arm tucked under the ribs and the elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm starting pointed out in front. Rotate the forearm up and inward across the body toward the chest, lifting the dumbbell, then lower under control. Gravity loads the inward rotation; keep the elbow tucked so the cuff works through its arc.
regional_bias: subscapularis (anterior cuff); free-weight version is light and peaks near the top of internal rotation
cues: Lie on the working-arm side, elbow tucked into the ribs, lift the dumbbell across by rotating the shoulder inward only. Very light load; do not let the torso roll or the elbow drift off the body.

name: Serratus Punch / Scapular Push-Up (Push-Up Plus)
rom_notes: From a plank or push-up top position with the elbows locked, protract the scapulae by pushing the floor away (the 'plus'), spreading the shoulder blades and rounding the upper back; then let the chest sink between the shoulder blades to retract. All motion is at the scapulae, not the elbows. The end-range protraction (push-up plus) is where serratus activation peaks. Can be regressed to hands-on-wall or quadruped, or loaded as a banded supine punch.
regional_bias: serratus anterior (the push-up-plus end range is its highest-activation drill); pec minor assists scapular tilt/protraction
cues: Keep the elbows straight the whole rep; the only movement is your shoulder blades sliding apart and together. Push the floor away hard at the top to round the upper back and load the serratus. Don't sag the hips or bend the arms into a normal push-up.

name: Supine Cable Scapular Protraction (Serratus Punch)
rom_notes: Lie supine (or set up against a low cable) with the arm extended straight up toward the ceiling and the elbow locked. Reach/punch the fist further toward the ceiling by protracting the scapula off the bench, then let it settle back into retraction. Open-chain version of the push-up plus; the locked elbow forces pure scapular travel and constant cable tension loads the full protraction arc. A dumbbell can substitute for cable with gravity providing resistance.
regional_bias: serraty anterior (isolated open-chain protraction); pec minor assists; minimal glenohumeral motion keeps it off the delts/pec major
cues: Keep the elbow locked and 'reach to the ceiling' from the shoulder blade only — the fist should travel a few centimeters further as the scapula protracts. Slow, controlled, light load; this is scapular-control work, not a press.

name: Wall Slide (Serratus Wall Slide)
rom_notes: Forearms (or a towel/foam roller) against a wall in a 'goalpost' position; slide the arms up the wall overhead while actively protracting and upwardly rotating the scapulae, then return. The combination of overhead reach plus protraction recruits the serratus through its upward-rotation force-couple role with the traps. A light band around the wrists or pressing into the wall increases serratus demand. Trains scapular upward rotation through a large overhead arc.
regional_bias: serratus anterior in its upward-rotation role (overhead range); low-load mobility/control drill rather than a hypertrophy driver
cues: Press the forearms into the wall and reach long as you slide up — feel the shoulder blades wrap forward and rotate up, not shrug up. Keep the ribs down and lower back flat. Slow and deliberate; this is a control drill.

name: Overhead Shrug (Scapular Upward-Rotation Shrug)
rom_notes: Hold a light load locked out overhead (barbell, dumbbells, or in a Smith machine) with the elbows straight. Shrug/press the shoulder blades upward into full upward rotation and elevation (reaching the weight higher toward the ceiling), then lower the scapulae under control. The overhead position makes the serratus and upper traps co-act to upwardly rotate the scapula. Elbows stay locked so motion is scapular, not elbow extension.
regional_bias: serratus anterior + upper trapezius force couple for scapular upward rotation in the overhead position; trains lockout stability for pressing
cues: Lock the elbows and press the bar another inch higher by reaching through the shoulder blades, then let them settle down. Keep the ribcage down and don't bend the arms. Light load with overhead stability requirements — build up gradually.

name: Scapular Dip / Straight-Arm Depression
rom_notes: Support the body on parallel bars (or dip handles / a captain's chair) with the elbows locked straight. Let the shoulders rise toward the ears (scapular elevation), then drive the shoulders down away from the ears by depressing and downwardly tilting the scapulae, raising the torso a few centimeters without bending the elbows. Pure scapular depression/anterior-tilt with the elbows locked; loads the pectoralis minor and lower traps. Distinct from a triceps dip (no elbow flexion).
regional_bias: pectoralis minor (scapular depression / anterior tilt) with lower-trap and serratus co-action; a small-ROM scapular-control drill, not a mass builder
cues: Lock the elbows and move only at the shoulder blades — sink into the shoulders, then push the body up by driving the shoulders down away from the ears. No elbow bend; if the elbows flex you've turned it into a dip.

name: Hip Adduction Machine
rom_notes: Seated, pads on the inner thighs/knees; let the legs spread to a strong stretched (abducted) start, then squeeze the thighs together to full adduction. The machine isolates the frontal-plane adduction function with constant tension; emphasize the lengthened range.
regional_bias: adductor longus/brevis and gracilis (short adductors) with adductor magnus assisting; upright torso biases the proximal adductors. Open the pads to a deep abducted stretch for full ROM.
cues: Set a wide abducted start for a deep inner-thigh stretch, squeeze the legs together under control, pause briefly at the closed position; keep the torso upright and let the adductors (not momentum) do the work.

name: Cable Standing Hip Adduction
rom_notes: Ankle cuff on a low pulley, stand side-on with the working leg abducted out to the side; pull the leg across the body toward and past the midline against constant cable tension. One leg at a time through a full adduction sweep.
regional_bias: adductor longus/brevis (frontal-plane adductors) with adductor magnus; single-leg loading lets the working leg start in a deep abducted stretch.
cues: Stand tall and braced, let the leg drift out for a stretch, then sweep it across the body squeezing the inner thigh; don't lean the torso or hike the hip to cheat the rep.

name: Copenhagen Plank / Adduction
rom_notes: Side-lying with the top foot/shin on a bench and the bottom leg hanging; raise the pelvis so the top adductors support bodyweight. Performed as a held isometric (short-lever knee-on-bench to long-lever foot-on-bench progression) or with controlled hip adduction reps of the bottom leg toward the bench.
regional_bias: adductor longus/brevis and adductor magnus of the top (supporting) leg, loaded heavily in a lengthened position; doubles as anti-lateral-flexion core work. A well-supported eccentric/lengthened adductor stimulus.
cues: Top shin/foot on the bench, drive the top inner thigh down into the bench to lift the hips into a straight line; keep the torso from sagging. Regress by bending the top knee onto the bench, progress to a straight-leg foot-on-bench long lever.

name: Banded Hip Adduction
rom_notes: Anchor a band out to the side at ankle height, loop it around the working ankle while standing side-on; pull the leg in across the midline against band tension. Can also be done side-lying with a band around the thighs. Resistance increases as the leg adducts (ascending).
regional_bias: adductor longus/brevis with adductor magnus; band tension is light and ascending, so best as activation/prehab rather than a heavy hypertrophy driver.
cues: Keep constant inward tension, sweep the leg across the body and squeeze the inner thigh, resist the band on the way back out; brace the trunk and avoid swinging.

name: Hip Abduction Machine (Gluteus Minimus / TFL Bias)
rom_notes: Seated upright, pads on the outer thighs; press the knees apart through full abduction. Sitting tall and slightly reclined targets the deeper gluteus minimus and the TFL (an anterior abductor/hip flexor) rather than the upper glute max fibers a forward lean recruits.
regional_bias: gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae as deep/anterior frontal-plane abductors; an upright torso (vs. leaning forward, which biases upper GMax) keeps emphasis on the minimus/TFL. Full ROM out to a strong abducted squeeze.
cues: Sit tall (don't lean forward), drive the knees apart to a full outer squeeze, control the return; the upright posture keeps the load on the deep minimus and TFL.

name: Cable Standing Hip Abduction (TFL / Minimus Bias)
rom_notes: Ankle cuff on a low pulley, stand side-on; raise the working leg out to the side and a touch forward against constant cable tension. The slightly-forward line of pull recruits the anterior gluteus minimus and TFL more than a straight-back lateral raise.
regional_bias: gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae; raising the leg out and slightly forward (rather than out-and-back, which favors GMax/medius) emphasizes the anterior abductors. Constant cable tension through ROM.
cues: Stand tall and braced, lift the leg out and slightly in front of the hip, squeeze, control down; keep the pelvis level and avoid leaning the torso to cheat.

name: Banded Lateral Walk
rom_notes: Loop a band around the knees or ankles, sit into a quarter-squat (hips back, knees out), then take controlled lateral steps maintaining outward band tension the whole time so the trailing leg never collapses inward.
regional_bias: gluteus minimus and TFL plus medius as frontal-plane abductors/pelvic stabilizers; band tension is light and ascending, so it functions mainly as activation and pelvic-stability prehab. Each step is a unilateral abduction against the band.
cues: Stay low in a partial squat, keep constant outward band tension, step wide and resist the band as the trailing leg follows; don't let the knees cave or the torso bob up and down.

name: Side-Lying Hip Abduction
rom_notes: Lie on your side, bottom leg bent for stability; raise the straight top leg through full hip abduction against gravity (and an ankle weight or band). Lifting the leg slightly in front of the body biases the anterior abductors; keep the pelvis stacked and from rolling back.
regional_bias: gluteus minimus and TFL plus gluteus medius; lifting the top leg with a slight forward/internal-rotation lean targets the anterior minimus/TFL, while a neutral/slightly-back lift favors the posterior medius. Loadable with an ankle weight or band for a real stimulus.
cues: Stack the hips, lead with the heel, raise the top leg to full abduction without rolling the pelvis backward; pause at the top, lower slowly. Add an ankle weight or band once bodyweight is easy.

name: Banded Ankle Inversion
rom_notes: Anchor a band to the outside of the working foot (or loop it around both feet); with the leg extended and ankle neutral, turn the sole inward (inversion) against band tension through full medial range, then control back to neutral. Small-amplitude, deliberate reps.
regional_bias: tibialis posterior (primary inverter and medial-arch support) with tibialis anterior assisting; a low-load prehab drill for medial ankle resilience and arch support rather than hypertrophy.
cues: Keep the lower leg still and move only at the ankle, turning the sole inward against the band; pause at end-range inversion and control the return. Light tension, high control — this is a tendon/stabilizer drill.

name: Banded Ankle Eversion
rom_notes: Anchor a band to the inside of the working foot (or cross it from the opposite side); with the leg extended and ankle neutral, turn the sole outward (eversion) against band tension through full lateral range, then control back to neutral. Small-amplitude, deliberate reps.
regional_bias: fibularis (peroneal) group as the primary everters and lateral ankle stabilizers; a low-load prehab drill targeting lateral-ankle-sprain resilience rather than size.
cues: Hold the shin still and move only at the ankle, turning the sole outward against the band; pause at end-range eversion, control back. Light tension, high control — key prehab against rolled (inversion-sprained) ankles.

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise (Ankle-Stabilizer Focus)
rom_notes: Forefoot on a block or floor, single leg, performed unsupported (free hand off the wall) to force the deep invertors/everters to keep the ankle tracking straight while you raise to full plantarflexion and lower into a controlled dorsiflexion stretch. The instability — not just the load — is the stimulus.
regional_bias: tibialis posterior and the fibularis group as medial/lateral ankle stabilizers controlling inversion-eversion drift during a single-leg raise (gastrocnemius/soleus/plantaris drive the plantarflexion itself). Distinct from the gastroc-primary single-leg calf raise: here the goal is frontal-plane ankle control, balance, and arch/stabilizer strength.
cues: Go unsupported to challenge balance; keep the ankle from rolling in or out as you raise and lower — that medial-lateral control is the whole point. Drive straight up the second toe, full stretch at the bottom. Add a light dumbbell only once the ankle tracks cleanly.
